DATA ANALYSIS · INFORMATION DESIGN · 2026

Expensive rent.
A bigger story.

Why is renting harder to afford in some Toronto neighbourhoods? I explored 140 neighbourhoods to show what price alone leaves out.

THE QUESTION THAT CHANGED MY PROJECT

Where is rent highest?
→ Where is the pressure greatest?

CONTEXT
Academic data storytelling project
MY WORK
Data preparation, analysis & visual narrative
TOOLS & DATA
Excel · Tableau · 2011 & 2016 profiles
01 The question02 The evidence03 Behind the work04 What I learned

01 / FINDING THE STORY

I started with price.
Then asked a better question.

My first idea was to find the most expensive places to live in Toronto. But a price ranking could not tell me how difficult housing was to afford. It also could not tell me why people chose an area.

I narrowed the question to something the data could answer: how do rental costs, income and housing support relate to housing pressure?

The shift: from ranking expensive places to explaining an uneven experience.

A QUICK WAY INTO THE DATA

Same bill.
Different breathing room.

A $1,200 monthly housing bill takes 40% of a $3,000 income, but 20% of a $6,000 income. The price is identical. The pressure is not.

Illustrative budgets, not observed households. Before-tax income.

$3,000 monthly income

$6,000 monthly income

Blue = $1,200 for housing. “Pressure” below means spending at least 30% of income on housing.

02 / FOLLOW THE EVIDENCE

First, locate the pressure.

The map shows the share of renters spending at least 30% of income on housing. Darker blue means more renters cross that threshold. It shows where pressure is concentrated, without claiming to explain why.

60.3%

of renter households in Newtonbrook West crossed the threshold, compared with 36.1% in Kingsway South. Pressure appears in different parts of the city.

THE SURPRISE

The higher bill did not mean
the greater strain.

Read right for higher housing costs; read up for more renters above the 30% threshold. Each dot is one neighbourhood. Hover over a dot to see its values.

NEWTONBROOK WEST

$1,135 / month

60.3% of renters above the threshold

KINGSWAY SOUTH

$1,640 / month

36.1% of renters above the threshold

Kingsway South had a higher average housing bill, but fewer renters above the threshold. Price alone is an incomplete explanation.

LOOKING FOR CONTEXT

Income is part of the picture.
Housing support is, too.

Regent Park and South Parkdale make the story concrete. Regent Park had a lower typical household income, yet lower rental costs and a smaller share of renters under pressure.

2011 · Income covers all households; rental costs, support and pressure cover renters. Read each measure separately: units differ.

More subsidized housing and lower costs may help explain the difference. This neighbourhood comparison does not prove that support alone caused it.
A separate 2016 lens: why I did not draw a trend line

The project’s 2016 overview shows 36.6% of assessed Toronto households spending at least 30% of income on housing. It includes owners and renters. The 2011 analysis above covers renters only.

Because the populations differ, these percentages cannot show whether renter affordability improved or worsened. Both years are historical snapshots, not today’s rental market.

03 / BEHIND THE WORK

Making the analysis
easier to follow.

  1. Narrow the question

    I moved from “Where is it expensive?” to a focused affordability question. I dropped “willing to pay” because the data does not measure preferences.

  2. Make the measures comparable

    I organized the cleaned tables by neighbourhood, kept the two census years separate, and made the units explicit: dollars, percentages and percentage points.

  3. Choose a visual for each question

    The map locates pressure. The dot chart challenges the price-only story. The paired comparison adds income and housing-support context.

  4. Edit for a reader

    I replaced broad chart titles with takeaway headlines and added reading guides. Every visual now advances the same story.

04 / WHAT I LEARNED

A useful data story
changes the question.

The outcome is a focused visual explanation: affordability depends on how housing costs meet people’s resources. The project taught me to question an easy headline, keep different populations visible, and give each chart one clear job.

What I would do next

Use a consistent, newer dataset with renter-specific income and comparable boundaries. That would support a stronger time comparison and avoid treating all-household income as a renter’s actual budget.
